speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to bring to the attention of the house apd the government a matter which is of supreme importance to the basic indus-

I cannot hear you very well, either, Mr. Speaker; I thank you for asking for better order. As I say, the Dominion cerealist may receive a maximum of $3,480 and house allowance of possibly $30 or $40 a month. I want to say a few words regarding the work of the cereal division.

Technical Officials-Mr. Coote

maintopic: SUPPLY-SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS
speechtext:
I would ask hon. members kindly to be silent; I cannot hear the hon. gentleman at all.
Mr. C'OOTE: One of the most important activities of the cereal division is that of evolving and developing varieties of wheat capable of producing maximum yields of high quality throughout the various wheat growing districts of western Canada. The world famous marquis wheat is the most outstanding-ing contribution of this division to date. According to conservative estimates we now realize in Canada at least $100,000,000 more from our wheat crop annually than would have been possible had we still to depend on the varieties of wheat grown prior to the introduction of marquis. Many districts however require varieties that have earlier maturing qualities than marquis, and the introduction of garnet wheat in 1920 and reward wheat this year seems to have filled that want. Both these wheats are the work of men engaged in the cereal branch. The breeding of rust-resistant varieties, which is largely concentrated at the rust research laboratory in Winnipeg, where it is being prosecuted by officials of the cereal division co-operating with Dominion plant pathologists, is an immensely important undertaking. As is well known, rust has exacted a toll of as high as $100,000,000 in a single year. Indeed, many farmers in Manitoba and parts of Saskatchewan have almost been compelled to abandon their farms as the result of the frequent occurence of this dread disease. The solution of this problem, would appear to be possible, providing the personnel of the staff be held intact. Unfortunately a serious depletion in the staff has already taken place -through the resignation of one of the most outstanding officials, and I understand that other resignations are pending unless salaries are adjusted.
I wish to quote a few sentences from the Grain Growers' Guide in regard to the discrimination which seems to exist so far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned. The statement is made:
As for younger men the situation is well illustrated by an incident referred to in the March issue of Scientific Agriculture. Recently the commission advertised for two men. For an assistant superintendent for an experimental farm, who must be an agricultural college graduate, with a post graduate degree and special training in histology, genetics and physiology, it offered a salary range of $1,620 to $1,920. For an assistant chief of the narcotics division, who is required to have only a high school education and two years' clerical experience, preferably police experience, with some knowledge of drugs, it offers a salary range of from $2,400 to $2,880. It is little wonder in these circumstances that Canada is losing some of her best scientific agriculturists.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS

speechtext:
We cannot afford to lose these men. I think it is generally admitted that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada, and wheat is certainly the greatest item in our agricultural economy. I want to quote briefly from an article entitled Wheat is King, published in MacLean's Magazine of April 1st:
The stupendous Canadian wheat industry totally eclipses all other Dominion enterprises in the number of men employed, in the amount of machinery utilized and in the quantity of money involved. When talking of Canadian wheat we now speak in terms of billions. . . . Wheat, and wheat alone, augments the national treasury annually by $100,000,000 more than the total annual income from our forests. It brings into Canada twice as much money as our mines, and ten times as much as our fisheries. No other single commodity produced in the Dominion has a chance in the race for national importance. It is so far ahead of all others that it has no competitors.
The greatest enemy of our wheat producers to-day is rust. In this connection I want t-o quote from an editorial which appeared in the Alberta Farmer:
Because the future success of western Canada's wheat harvests is seriously threatened the Dominion government, under pressure of public opinion, organized two years ago a Dominion rust research laboratory. It is not necessary to explain to prairie farmers the seriousness of the rust menace. A year ago 55 per cent of the wheat crop of the west graded No. 3 northern or better; this year only 35 per cent of the crop graded that high. The cause for the most part was rust. Thus far this year only one and one-half per cent of the wheat graded in western Canada has been classed No. 1 northern and only 10 per cent No. 2 northern. The cause for the most part has been rust. Rust is responsible for the fact that in 1927 Manitoba, which was at one time an exclusive bread wheat area produced oyer 50 per cent of durum wheat. 'Rust was almost entirely responsible for the reduction of 20,000,000 bushels in Manitoba's wheat crop last year from the year before. Absence of rust in Alberta during 1927 made it possible for this province to raise as much wheat on six and one-half million acres as Saskatchewan, where rust was rampant, raised on thirteen million acres. Stem rust caused a loss of approximately two hundred million dollars to prairie farmers in 1916.
Even if that statement is exaggerated it should cause some concern to this house. It seems to me that this is the proper time to place before the house a resolution passed by the Canadian Council of Agriculture at its annual meeting, which was held in Winnipeg last March:
Whereas grain rust is costing the country millions of dollars annually, which loss can only be prevented through the agency of scientific research, which demands the services of the most highly trained experts;
And whereas Canada is losing many agricultural scientists to other countries where the scale of remuneration is considerably higher than prevails here;

Technical Officials-Mr. Coote
And whereas the civil service salary classification sharply discriminates against scientific men engaged in agricultural research work as compared with men requiring no higher standard of training engaged in other branches of the civil service;
And whereas the future prosperity of Canada depends in a large measure upon scientific research in the various branches of agricultural development;	,
Therefore the Canadian Council of Agriculture recommends to the federal government that immediate steps be taken to remove the discrimination against agricultural scientists now existing in the civil service salary classification;
And further that nothing be allowed to stand in the way of prosecuting rust research work as rapidly as possible to a successful conclusion.
At present the obstacle in the way is the insufficient salaries which are being paid to men engaged in this work; according to the press we have been losing quite a number of men who were formerly actively engaged in this work at Winnipeg. The first of these of whom mention is made is Doctor D. L. Bailey, who had charge of the laboratory; he has been asked by the university of Toronto to accept a position as head of the department of pathology. Next is Mr. J. R. Craigie, who has accepted invitations from the United States Botanical Society at Washington and from Harvard university to present his paper and to consider opportunities they have to offer. I understand that he has accepted one of the offers. After nine years of intensive training, he started work at the rust laboratory for $2,400 per year, and his maximum salary under the present 'classification would be $2,880. The next is Doctor Margaret Newton, who has a standing offer from the university of Saskatchewan. Doctor C. H Goulding also has received offers from the United States. It is unfortunate but true that during the last few years many highly trained scientific officers have left our service to go to the United States or other countries because they have been offered higher salaries; our Department of Agriculture alone has lost over 75 professional officers in the last five years. Many of these men go to the United States and enter either the federal service or one of the various state services, and unless these salaries are increased we will lose many more of these trained investigators and professional officers. When these men leave the sendee they take with them a wealth of knowledge and experience which in many cases cannot be replaced.
Among those who have left the service within the last few years are two highly trained scientific officers, each holding a doctor's degree. These men resigned from the entomological branch of the Department of Agri-
IMr. Coote.]
culture three years ago, one to accept a position in the United States federal service at $4,500 per year and the other to accept a position in the Fiji islands at $7,500. It does , seem a strange thing to me that this country cannot afford to pay our men salaries equal to what they can get in the Fiji islands. These men were each receiving $2,760 in Canada, and the maximum of that class since has been raised to $2,880. One of these positions is still vacant; it has been advertised several times but no suitable person has applied. These gentlemen were investigating the injury done by the spruce bud worm in the forests of eastern Canada, with a view to devising methods of preventing similar outbreaks. It' is stated that in our eastern forests the spruce bud worm has killed fir, balsam and spruce within the last twenty years to the amount of from 150,000,000 to 200,000,000 cords, worth between one and two billion dollars before being manufactured into pulp.
A few months ago we were informed that a highly trained technical officer in charge of the tobacco division at the experimental farm had resigned from our service to accept a much higher salary under the Australian council for scientific research. Our scientific branches are just as important as those of the United States, Australia, or the Fiji islands; our problems are quite as difficult to solve. _ It is necessary that our scientific investigations be maintained at a standard of efficiency equal to that of any other country, and this can be done only by retaining these highly trained men in our service. Doctor Charles Saunders, through his discovery of marquis wheat, is credited with having increased the value of our wheat crop to the extent of $100,000,000 annually; this parliament has seen fit to grant Doctor Saunders a pension in recognition of his services, but who knows whether by losing men of this character to other countries because of the inadequate salaries we are paying, we may not have lost men who could have rendered to agriculture in Canada services equally valuable to those rendered by Doctor Saunders?

speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
tell me the pension given Doctor Saunders?
Mr. COOTE; I am sorry, but I cannot give that; I do not expect that it is^ equal to the pension given some of our judges, however.
I do not wish to take up the time of the house unnecessarily to-day, Mr. Speaker. In closing I wish to say that I have brought this matter up for discussion because I believe it to be very' important in a truly national sense that the salaries of these men should be put on a more satisfactory basis before

Technical Officials-Mr. Steedsman
this parliament prorogues. I hope we may have a promise from the government that this will be done and that the supplementary estimates will provide for such increases in these salaries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS
speechtext:
I
feel grateful to my hon. friend for having introduced this subject. I was under the impression that it might be discussed on another occasion, but now that it has been introduced I would like to say a few words with reference to it. I am not going into a comparison of the salaries paid in the different branches here with those paid in other countries for services of a scientific character; my hon. friend has done that already, and in presenting what I have to say I wish to be as brief as possible.
We have been alarmed by the fact that we have lost many of our best scientists because we have been unable to offer them salaries sufficiently large to induce them to stay here. The question introduced to-day by my hon. friend is one of the most important which will come before this parliament this session. We realize that the prosperity of this country depends to a very great degree upon the success of agriculture, and the invasion of the grain fields of western Canada by rust is threatening the whole prosperity of the country. We find the area affected spreading from year to year; a few years ago the ravages of this disease were confined to Manitoba, but now we find it spreading considerably farther afield. It is almost certain, unless some means are found to control or combat this menace, that the whole area of western Canada will be more or less affected. I will be pardoned if I confine my remarks chiefly to the effect it has had in Manitoba, the province from which I come.
As the hon. gentleman has just said, the wheat crop in Manitoba last year amounted to only 30,000,000 bushels, and of that amount 15,000,000 bushels were durum wheat. The remainder was of a very poor quality, so low in fact that much of it was almost unsalable, being little better than feed wheat. The introduction of new varieties and the propagation of rust-resistant varieties has done something to relieve the situation. Great areas in southwestern Manitoba, from which I come, have had to change from marquis to durum wheat. While this has proven very satisfactory for that particular locality, at the same time we can readily understand that it is out of the question that any one variety of wheat will be satisfactory for the whole of western Canada. Climatic and soil
conditions make that impossible, and the question of markets has also been mentioned by my hon. friend. While there are those who suggest that the introduction of new varieties and the propagation of rust-resistant varieties may be the solution, I am not prepared to go that far, for the reason that no one or two varieties of wheat can be suitable for such an extensive area as we have in western Canada to-day.
. Other kinds of grain are being affected as well. Not only was the wheat crop of Manitoba affected last year by rust, but the oat crop also suffered, and to a greater degree. The oat crop of Manitoba last year was cut down by two-thirds from the previous year, due largely to rust, aggravated, of course, by weather conditions. The balance of the crop was of very poor quality, scarcely any of it fit for feed. Great quantities of feed and seed oats have had to be imported into Manitoba this year as a result of the attacks of rust on the oat crop last year.
So you will see that it extends ever farther than wheat. When it comes to affect the feed grains of our province or our country, you will see that our whole agriculture is affected. As a result of the condition I have outlined with regard to oats, you will find that very few cattle were fed in Manitoba this last winter. A great number of stock which would otherwise have stayed there has been shipped out as the result of the failure of that crop, owing to rust.
I do not wish to detatin the house but I want to point out to the government the importance of securing the very best men available, the most highly trained scientific men that it is possible to find anywhere, to take on this. work. And having secured them we should pay them such remuneration as will induce them to stay with the job. At the present time Canada cannot afford to lose one man who can do anything towards the solution of this problem, by not paying him sufficient money to keep him at his post. Therefore I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture and to the government not only the advisability but the necessity of paying sufficient wages to induce these men to carry on this work which means so much to the prosperity of this country..

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS
speechtext:
My hon. friend' from Victoria closed his remarks with the statement that the responsibility was the government's. I beg to submit on behalf of the government that we realize the importance of this question, and we are sympathetic to the idea of retaining within the service the very best men and women obtainable at the salaries provided. But may I point out at once to you, Mr. Speaker, and

Technical Officials-Mr. Robl
to the house that it is the Civil Service Commission. that fixes the salaries for the employees of the Dominion of Canada. We have in the Dominion of Canada many departments of public service, and the Civil Service Commission, like the government, must always keep in mind when adjusting salaries, how any proposed increases or decreases in one department will affect other departments. I believe that all parties entrusted with the responsibility of office have always endeavoured to keep in the public service competent and industrious employees who were interested in the affairs of the country. But we have lost excellent civil servants. I can recall that we have lost from the public service of Canada two or three men who left many years ago to go into private business, and I admit frankly that one or two of the three I have in mind are much better off, in a monetary sense, to-day than if they had remained in the public service. But as I said a moment ago, it is not the government that fixes the salaries generally all along the line in the departments. In the first place, recommendations come from the Civil Service Commission to the treasury board. It may interest the house to know that we did receive from the Civil Service Commission on the 23rd day of May last, just seven days ago, just three days before the supplementary estimates were tabled, certain recommendations regarding the technical and professional men and women in the public service. I have read that recommendation carefully, and I observe that even the Civil Service Commission, having given considerable study to this question, and realizing, as I believe they do realize, the importance of an increase in the salaries of the technical and professional staff, but realizing also the difficulties, are not yet quite clear in their own minds what should be done. For the information of the house I will just read a summary of the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission:
The recommendation is that the minimum and maximum salary rates for professional and scientific classes and for other classes with a maximum salary of $4,000 or more he revised, and increases according to a general plan, subject to such modifications as the committee consider warranted-
That was the view presented to the government by the Civil Service Commission only seven days ago, and as I said, they are not yet quite clear in their own minds, because to summarize:
The commission is as yet none too clear what classes should get increases. In one paragraph they comment on the fact that if increases are given to the scientific men only, it may result
in cases where the heads of branches might be receiving less than their assistants, so that increases would have to be made not only in the salaries of the scientific men, but also like increases for all positions where the salary is over $4,000.
But if the commission had any doubt in their own minds as to what classes should be increased, they had no doubt as to what the cost would be to the taxpayers of the Dominion, because in this memorandum they state that on the basis of the estimated increases which they are now considering it would involve an additional outlay of $750,000 a year. I am not sure that that would be sufficient to keep in the service the scientific men that have been referred to this afternoon, because the Civil Service Commission say that upon this basis the increases vary from $240 for classes with maximum salary rates of less than $2,400 per annum, to $420 for classes with maximum rates greater than $4,000.
Those increases might be considered by some of these officials who have been offered other positions insufficient to retain them in the service. When my hon. friend says that the responsibility is the government's, I say that we are willing to take all the responsibility that is coming to us, but we have a Civil Service Commission that revises and recommends the salaries to be paid to civil servants, and if we increase the salaries and come back next session with an increased vote of $750,000 for carrying on the business of the country, I wonder if we shall be attacked.
The government welcome this discussion and the co-operation of all classes to assist us in retaining in the service those who are most useful to the country.	But before going
further may I say this? Taking them generally, the Dominion of Canada has a pretty good staff of civil servants. The men and women are devoted to the national service, and the Dominion provides very well for them. The civil service-and I am speaking generally now-receive in remuneration a return that compares most favourably with their brothers' and sisters' who are paying the taxes and paying their salaries. Not only do they receive pretty good salaries, but once a man or woman is on a permanent basis he or she has the assurance of continuing a civil servant, no matter what government may be in power, so long as the service rendered is loyal and efficient. And civil servants have the further advantage of being entitled to a pension when they reach a certain age limit, and in case of death a certain proportion of the pension is continued to their widows. So those who have the responsibilities of bringing up a family are fairly well provided for.

Technical Officials-Mr. Rohb
It will be found that the salaries of our professional and technical civil servants compare very favourably with the salaries earned by other technical and professional men outside the service.

speechtext:
Would the minister permit
this question:	In regard to the duty of the
Civil Sendee Commission to revise salaries, have the commission authority to revise any salaries until the matter is referred to them by the government or by the heads of departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS
speechtext: I am speaking from memory, and subject to correction, but my understanding is that the head of a department suggests to the Civil Service Commission the desirability of reclassifying certain employees. speechtext:
May I ask this question:
If the number of able veterinarians continues to reduce at the rate of 25 per cent, as it has done since 1919, where in the future are we going to get our supply of professional men for the health of animals branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS
speechtext:
My hon. friend is better
posted on that than I am, but my principal difficulty with veterinarians is to find them government jobs. If any vacancies occur I think I could find a few veterinarians ready to fill them. Allow me to read part of paragraph 2 of the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission to council, so it may be on record for the information of the house: The Civil Service Commission find that the distinction between the professional and scientific positions and other positions of the service is that for all professional and scientific positions the basic qualification requirement is education equivalent to graduation from a university or college of recognized standing. Therefore, in determing what classes should be included in this revision, the controlling factor considered has been whether or not the work of an employee, to enable him to carry on properly the duties of his position, requires university graduation or its equivalent. It therefore follows that it is those classes for which university graduation or its equivalent are essential qualifications, which will now be subject to revision.
That brings up another question of possible difficulty. There are men and women who have been many years in the service, and their long experience makes them peculiarly useful in attending to the country's affairs. Is it fair that they should be discriminated against because they did not have the advan-
tage of a college education? They have been through what is perhaps the best of all universities-the university of experience within the service.
I do not wish to detain the house any longer. I repeat, the government is sympathetic in its attitude to the civil service, and is just as desirous as any former government to retain the services of those who are useful in carrying on the business of the country. But I ask the house:	The government having
received this memorandum from the Civil Service Commission just seven days ago, and three days before the supplementary estimates were tabled, is it reasonable to expect that ministers-who work as long hours as many civil servants, that is, about eighteen hours a day-could give this matter in the closing days of the session the consideration which it deserves. The government will go carefully into the question of salaries, not only of those engaged in the Department of Agriculture but in all departments. May I say in passing that the Civil Service Commission recognize the importance of the Department of Agriculture, for I notice in their memorandum this statement is made:
There is urgent need for an immediate special review of all scientific and professional classes in the Department of Agriculture. Such review should be supplementary to any increase granted to such classes hereby and will be reported to His Excellency the Governor General in council at the earliest possible date.
We have not had that yet, but when it does come to us We will look into it carefully.
Only one word more in conclusion. My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) made a comparision between salaries paid to our civil servants and those paid in the United States. I submit that, generally speaking, our civil service is remunerated just about as well as that of the United States. But if my hon. friend is going to compare salaries in the United States and Canada, perhaps it would be interesting to some of hs own friends, from whom I have heard *whispers in this regard, if he would compare the salaries of congressmen and senators in the United States with indemnities paid members of parliament and senators in Canada. He might compare the salaries of the judiciary in the United States with salaries paid judges in this Dominion.
The government are charged with the responsibility which my hon. friend has just indicated. But we have a responsibility not only in taking care of our professional and scentific men in the service but, as well, in seeing to it that there shall be such uniformity throughout the service as will be satisfactory

Technical Officials-Mr. Millar
to all classes. I repeat, we are sympathetic to increases in salaries where they are deserved by those doing useful scientific work, and we welcome this discussion, which will be carefully considered during the recess.

maintopic: SUPPLY-SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS
speechtext:
The
hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) and the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Steedsman) well said that no more important matter has been brought to the attention of .the house this session than the question introduced by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). I am not going to cover the ground already covered so well by the hon. member for Macleod and others who have spoken, but I want to add a word in support of what they have said.
The losses which Canada is sustaining at the present time through the lack of research are so enormous that this matter must be looked upon very seriously. The hon. member for Macleod spoke of rust. I want to stress this because it is one of the greatest enemies which the western wheat grower has to face to-day. In Manitoba, a province already referred to by the hon. member for Souris, the acreage under wheat in 1925 or 1926 was only the same as the acreage of 1903. That is a rather remarkable statement. The greatest factor in bringing about that state of affairs, forcing Manitoba into the growing of course grains and compelling that province very largely to go out of wheat production, has been rust. That disease has spread over Saskatchewan also, permeating almost the entire province. Last year it was pitiable to see crops of wheat which ordinarily should thresh forty bushels to the acre reduced by rust alone to such a condition as to yield only about seventeen or eighteen bushels. There was a heavy crop of straw to Ibe handled and tied with twine and yet the yield was very low. And not only was there a low yield, but the quality of grain was not as high.
It is no good exaggerating the losses sustained in this regard, but it is a very conservative estimate indeed that the loss annually from rust is $100,000,000. That is putting it low indeed. We have had some very excellent scientific men at work on the rust question. Until a few years ago scientists believed there was only one variety of rust; about the year 1916, however-I am speaking from memory-it was discovered that there was not one variety but there were forty. Twenty of these are found in western Canada. The little spores we see on wheat and other grain plants, falling on the plant work their way into it, cutting off the supply of food,
and they develop in such large numbers that they break out on the plant much the same as a rash on the human body. Then they go through a process whereby they multiply by hundreds of millions. The fact that there are twenty different varieties in western Canada makes it most difficult to find a remedy. Scientists tell us that the different spores- the different varieties-cannot be distinguished except by means of research, to discover the kind of plant on which they will feed. One will feed on one variety and another on some other variety, and that is the only way to distinguish them. So that now instead of having to fight, as formerly it was believed, merely one enemy, there are twenty to cope with. You can see therefore how difficult the problem becomes.
In the course of the session there has been considerable discussion about the loss to Canada through the importation of strawberries from the United States as well as other fruits from various places and eggs from China. I assure you that in the rust disease you have an importation infinitely worse. It comes from the United States, from the south, and it is a million times more harmful than any strawberries that come into this country. These spores travel in the air at a rapid pace, finding their way into the extreme north as far as Norway House and York Factory. They travel high as well as low in the air, two or three miles. To build a fence to keep them from coming up from the south is an impossibility. They must be fought by other mean*.
These research men in the service of Canada have made splendid headway, having found out a great deal about rust during the last ten or fifteen years, and it does seem to be most unfortunate that we should lose their sendees which means so much to the country. The evil is worse now than it was five or ten years ago and to lose these men because of insufficient remuneration, allowing them to go elsewhere, is a very grave mistake.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) suggests that the result of an increase in the salaries paid these men-at least I inferred as much from his remarks-would be something like $750,000, for the reason that if the salaries of the scientific men were increased this would have its effect all along the line. I agree with the minister that generally speaking our civil servants are very well paid. But when we have in our employ a man whose efforts mean not hundreds of thousands but millions of dollars to Canada, I contend that he is in a class that should be taken entirely out of

the civil service. Such a man should not be in the civil service but should be paid according to the service he is rendering to the state. And this should have no effect on the various classes in the civil service. I do not see any reason why scientific men such as those referred to by the hon. member for Macleod should not have their remuneration increased in order that we may retain their services, without that affecting the men who run elevators in our public buildings or elsewhere.
We have had a committee working for some months on the question of immigration; I think immigration is linked up with this matter, although very few of our students of immigration seem to realize that the reason we cannot get immigrants as easily as we would like is because conditions on the farm are not as attractive as they should be. I remember that on one occasion the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) remarked that these same hard conditions obtained thirty or forty years ago. The farmer has seen hard conditions; he has managed to weather them successfully, but that hardly applies at present. Now the farmer has more of class consciousness; he realizes that during the years gone by he has not enjoyed that share of the good things to which he was entitled. If he is going to work long hours and spend . his time in an employment which is very risky, which might be called almost a gamble, then he wants some remuneration to compensate him for that hard work and the lack of an opportunity to enjoy the good things which our city friends enjoy. We have arrived at a time when farmers' sons are not going to stay on the land unless conditions are made more attractive. If the amount of money we lose through rust alone could be saved, farming would pay so much better than is the case at present that it would become attractive, and some of the millions of dollars we are spending to bring immigrants into Canada could be saved.
I am very glad the hon. member for Macleod brought up this question; this may or may not be the best time for it, but I am not worrying about that. There is no wrong time to bring up a matter of such vital importance as this question of retaining the services of our scientific workers. Perhaps the government may not be altogether to blame for the situation, but I hope that something may be done, either by taking these men out from under the Civil Service Commission or in some other way, to retain their services which we so greatly need. The best are none too good for us, and I do not
IMr. Millar.]
want to see good men lost to us after they have spent years at their work which means that new and untried men must be employed, who require years to reach the same point in their work. This is a matter of very great importance, and I hope the government will give it the most serious consideration.

I wish to say a
few words in connection with the discussion yesterday regarding the High Commissioner's

International Relations
office. I regret to say that a statement made by the Prime Minister on that occasion escaped my notice. At page' 3507 of Hansard the fight bon. gentleman is reported as having Said:
.... at a subsequent session the government may ask parliament to approve of the appointment of a financial comptroller. . . .
I entirely disagree with the suggestion that any such officer is needed; I should have noticed the statement yesterday and spoken about it at the time. Ordinarily the High Commissioner's office in London is simply a spending office, although it is quite true that at present there are accounts still open with foreign governments. During the war the High Commissioner's office had to deal with a great many large and important financial questions; these we had to talk over and settle with the British treasury and the British war office. The High Commissioner attended to these questions throughout the war, with the assistance of his office staff, without having to call in any expert assistance. That is all I have to say on the subject; I wish to take this opportunity of expressing my appreciation of the faithful and effective service given by the whole staff of that office during the war.

subsubtopic: RULING OF MR. SPEAKER ON MOTION TO REFER BACK REPORT OF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before I leave the chair I would like to give my ruling on the point of order raised a short time ago by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), with reference to the motion presented by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). The point of order was to the effect that when a committee made a final report, that report could not be amended unless the committee were revived.
I think under the present circumstances the word "final" should mean that the report should be considered final only when it is adopted by the house, because the house can always refer a report back to a committee with instructions to amend it in any particular. The hon. member has cited May, page 440, but it was the twelfth edition. In May, thirteenth edition, at page 488 appears the following;
Motions also may be made that the report be recommitted; or recommitted, with minutes
of proceedings, so far as they relate to a certain paragraph; or recommitted, and the order of reference amended;
There apears to be a difference between the later and older editions of May. Bourinot
says, at page 479:
A report may he referred back to a committee for further consideration, or with instructions giving them power to amend the same in any respect. In this way a committee may regularly reconsider and even reverse a decision it has previously arrived at.
In the present instance there is no question of reversing the conclusions of the report; it is simply a technical change in the number of printed copies to be published. There is a recent and very clear case in point-the famous report of the customs committee some two years ago. A final report was brought before the house on the 18th June, 1926. The following appears on page 4694 of Hansard, June 18th, 1926:
The special committee appointed to investigate the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise, beg leave to present the following as their third and final report:
That was not a standing committee, it was a special committee. The revival of a committee should take place when it is a special committee, if lit should take place at all, but when it is a standing committee it is different. A few days afterwards, on June 22, I find that an hon. gentleman well versed in the rules of the house, Mr. Stevens, seconded by Mr. Doucet, moved:
That the report be not now adopted, but that it be referred back to the special committee with instructions to add thereto the following clauses as subclauses to paragraph 6:
So that the practice in the Canadian parliament does not prevent a report, even if it is a final report, of either a special or, better still, a standing committee, being referred back to be amended. The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) quoted from Beauchesne. But Beauchesne, paragraph 672, says:
A report may be referred back to a committee for further consideration, or with instructions giving them power to amend the same m any respect. In this way a committee may regularly reconsider and even reverse a decision it has previously arrived at. B. 479.
Under these circumstances, my ruling is that the motion is in order, and if it is the desire of the house we will revert to motions and decide if it should be carried or not.
Is it the pleasure of the house to revert to motions, and that the motion presented by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) be carried?

I called the attention of the Minister of National Revenue last night to a matter on which I did not have the file, and I suggested to the minister that I intended to refer to that matter again on this vote.
The minister said last night that he was not aware that any letter had been received by -him or his department from Mr. Dumoulin. You will remember the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, this being a case regarding J. W. Dumoulin of Notre Dame des Bois. Dumoulin is a French Canadian who volunteered, at the outset of the war. He served with distinction in that regiment which brought fame and honour to the province of Quebec, the 22nd regiment. On his return when he had been wounded and partly incapacitated, through the instrumentality of some friends, he was recommended for appointment as a preventive officer of customs at Notre Dame des Bois. His appointment was made on or about the 23rd of April. 1919, and he served until the 25th of November, 1926. On that date he received a letter from the Department of Customs and Excise, marked file B.2589-11, as follows:
J. W. Dumoulin, Esq.,
Customs Excise Officer,
Notre Dame des Bois, Que.
Sir,
I have the honour to inform you that an order in council was passed on November 19, 1926, dispensing with your services as customs excise enforcement officer at Notre Dame des Bois for political partisanship in the last election contrary to section 32 of the Civil Service Act, and your services will therefore require to terminate immediately upon receipt of this letter.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
G. W. Taylor, Acting Deputy Minister*
Immediately on receipt of this letter Mr. Dumoulin wrote a letter to the Minister of Customs and Excise, of which letter I have a duplicate copy. It will be remembered that the present Minister of National Revenue was appointed to his office on September 25, 1926, and this letter is dated November 29, 1926. In reading this letter you will notice that there are some discrepancies in construction of language. The mother tongue of Mr. Dumoulin is French, and he has written this letter in English, but I wish that I could write French as well as he writes English. The letter is as follows:
The Hon. Minister of Customs and Excise.
Ottawa, Canada.
Sir,
I am in receipt of a letter from the Department of Customs and Excise, dispensing with my services as a customs and excise enforce-

Supply-National Revenue
ment officer at the preventive station of Notre Dame des Bois, Que., for political partisanship in the last election.
I absolutely deny the accusation; and not only as a Canadian citizen but as a disabled veteran of the great war, I should be given a chance of appeal and face my accusers.
I have been employed in the customs service for nearly eight years, and if my dismissal is carried on by your department as intended to, I will come to a conclusion that a man who is doing his duty without doing favours to nobody, creates enemies that will constantly try to ruin himself.
All I want is fair play, and that is the reason why, I anticipate your opinion on the subject, before going any further.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
J. W. Dumoulin.
Of that letter Mr. Dumoulin has not to this day received any acknowledgment. Not having received any acknowledgment, he wrote on December 16, 1926, to the president of his branch of the Great War Veterans' Association asking that the matter be brought to the attention of the government through the branch of the veterans at Ottawa. On the same date, December 16, 1926, he wrote the following letter from Notre Dame des Bois, Quebec;
Secretary-Treasurer, Civil Service Commission, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:-
Enclosed please find the following copies of letters:
Departmental letter dated November 25 dispensing with my services as customs and excise enforcement officer;
Letter to Minister of Customs and Excise dated November 29 for which I have received no reply;
Letter to President of G.W.V.A. Standstead branch.
Owing to the fact that I have been discharged from the service under false accusation, I appeal to the Civil Service Commission to grant me an inquest to find out if I am not the victim of some violators of the customs laws.
Wishing that my request will meet your approval.
I remain,
Your obedient servant,
J. W. Dumoulin.
Under date of December 23, 1926, the Civil Service Commission replied as follows;
Dear Sir:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 16th instant enclosing copies of a letter addressed to you by the department under date of November 25, 1926, advising you that your services as customs excise enforcement officer at Notre Dame des Bois, Que., had been dispensed with by order in council; a letter which you then addressed under date of November 29 to the Honourable the Minister of Customs and Excise, and a letter dated the 16th December to the president, Stanstead branch, G.W.V.A.
I regret that the Civil Service Commission is unable to give you any assistance in this matter as removals are entirely in the hands of the heads of departments. The Civil Service Commission is not in a position to institute any inquiry, or to take any steps towards your reinstatement.
Yours very truly,
W. Foran, Secretary.
J. W. Dumoulin, Esq.,
Notre Dame des Bois, P.Q.
The matter went on. Mr. Dumoulin received no reply from the department, but as the correspondence, which I will not read in full, shows oral communications were made by representatives of the soldiers' association to some officers in the department.

I think I should correct my hon. friend there. Myi recollection is, I think, fairly accurate in this regard, that the officers in the soldiers' organization sent a letter to the department, indeed, I think, to myself. Last night I concluded that the matter was closed and I have not since looked up the file, but I think a letter was received by myself from the organization on behalf of this man and a reply was made.

I do not wish to go into the correspondence, but it will show, as I proceed, that J. C. G. Herwig, adjustment officer, Canadian legion of the British Empire Service League, of the service bureau at Ottawa, says that he had placed certain representations before the department. I am not, however, insisting upon that at the moment.
I have a letter from Mr. Herwig himself acknowledging receipt of a letter.

Perhaps the matter was
dealt with by correspondence. In order to show the good faith of Mr. Dumoulin, I may say that under date of January 10, 1927, he writes to the veterans' association as follows pointing out his case:
In regard to my discharge from the customs service, it looks now as if the complaint was made upon a Conservative committee sign, which was hung across the road from the Conservative committee room to the house where the customs office is only rented. It is easy to understand that this complaint is ridiculous. I cannot be held responsible for what has been done in Notre Dame des Bois, during the last election as I was on relieving duty at the ports of Beebe Junction and Rock Island, and this can be easily found in the customs records.
I accept the minister's statement unreservedly, but I had understood that that fact was further communicated to some officer of the department.

Supply-National Revenue

I have no knowledge of
that.

If the minster says he
has no knowledge of it, I accept his statement unreservedly. Under date of February 10, 1027, Mr. Herwig, who was the adjustment officer of the legion at Ottawa, wrote this letter:
It may not be necessary for Comrade Dumou-lin to come to Ottawa at this stage to make his representations, but in order to open the case will he please forward to the Minister of Customs immediately a statutory declaration covering all the points which he wishes to brine forward?
As far as we can ascertain the specific charges against him relate to the streamer across the street from the customs building, and to active participation in the election by canvass, as we understand that certain statements have been made affecting him in this regard.
Having received that, Dumoulin made an affidavit himself and had made by his friends some affidavits which he forwarded to the Department of Customs. I have duplicate copies of some of these and I intend to read them to show his good faith in the matter. The first affidavit is as follows:
To Whom it may concern:
I, J. W. Dumoulin, do solemnly and truly swear, that I did not attend any political meeting or taken any part whatever in the last election.
Signed J. W. Dumoulin. Province of Quebec,
District of St .Francois,
Sworn before me at Notre Dame des Bois, this seventeenth day of February, 1927.
Signed L. Lavigne, Justice of the Peace.
Another affidavit is as follows:
To Whom it may concern:
I, J. C. Goudreau, proprietor of the building in which the customs house is rented, do solemnly and truly swear that J. W. Dumoulin then customs officer, had nothing to do with the streamer that was laid across the road from my house to another, furthermore the above mention officer was not in this locality during the election campaign.
Signed J. C. Goudreau. Province of Quebec,
District of St. Francois,
Sworn before me at Notre Dame des Bois, this seventeenth day of February, 1927.
Signed L. Lavigne, Justice of the Peace.
Another. affidavit:
To Whom it may concern:
I, Edgar Dumoulin, do solemnly and truly swear that J. W. Dumoulin was not responsible for the Conservative committee sign that was laid across the road from the building in which [Mr. Cahar 1
the customs office is located as he was absent during the last election.
Signed Edgar Dumoulin. Province of Quebec,
District of St. Francois,
Sworn before me at Notre Dame des Bois, this seventeenth day of February, 1927.
Signed L. Lavigne, Justice of the Peace.
Then there is this further affidavit which I regard as most important:
To Whom it may concern:
I, the undersigned, do solemnly declare and swear, that J. W. Dumoulin was not here during the last political campaign.
That the Conservative committee for this locality was held in my house.
That the Conservative committee sign was hung across the street from my house to Mr. J. C. Goudreau's house, my neighbour.
That one end of the said sign was tied up tp my neighbour's house under my instructions after having obtained his permission.
That neither J. W. Dumoulin nor the customs department had anything to do with this committee sign.
That I have seen a document bearing the name of the Liberal leader from this locality, Mr. Ludger Lavigne, stating that he had no knowledge of political activities from the part of Mr. J. W. Dumoulin during the said political campaign; and which document is supposed to be in the Liberal member's hands for Comptop county, for his information.
Signed T. Goudreau.
Sworn before me at Notre Dame des Bois, Que., this 21st day of February, 1927.
Signed L. Lavigne, Justice of the Peace.
I thought that this had been communicated to the department, but I believe, in view of the minister's statement, that it was not. To show his good faith, Mr. J. C. Goudreau wrote also to the president of the soldiers' association under date of Februay 21, 1927, in which letter he says:
It has come to my knowledge that Mr. J. W. Dumoulin, former customs officer of this port, has lost his position on account of a streamer that I personally permitted that one end of the said streamer be tied up to my house.
He is tlhe proprietor of the house mentioned before. He goes on:
I regret very much that such an ordinary action from my part had been imposed upon the above mentioned veteran.
Here is the case: I am the proprietor of the building in which the customs office was located. I have rented to the Canadian department only three rooms of this building that contains four tenements in all. I occupy myself the first tenement, so when they call this the customs building, it's wrong! It's only the customs office in my own building in which I live constantly. This being said, whoever is the customs officer, how can he be responsible for what I may do in such occasions? It's evident, that all these reports are false as the said officer was on relieving duty at the time.

Supply-National Revenue
Then later, on April 12, 1927, Mr. Herwig wrote from Ottawa, after, as we supposed, having had communication with the department, but I withdraw that because I have not definite knowledge. He writes:
It would seem that in order to clear him it will be necessary to have the member retract.
That is the member of the House of Commons representing Compton county. He goes on to suggest that Mr. Dumoulin should see the member and have him retract. Then on April 16, 1927, Mr. Dumoulin wrote to the Department of Finance, as follows: Notre-Dame des Bois, Que.,
April 16th, 1927.
Department of Finance,
Ottawa, Canada.
Sirs:
As I have been dismissed from customs service in November last, for alleged political partisanship, (accusation I have denied and could not get inquiry), I apply to your department for refund of my superannuation funds.
Having waited five months for the said inquiry, no need to say that I expect this refund at once.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) J. W. Dumoulin.
On April 21, there is a statement which I am going to read, not because it involves the department, but because it is a matter that should be brought to the notice of the hon. member for Compton. Mr. Dumoulin writes the president of the soldiers' association under date of April 21, in which letter he says:
I have seen the member for Compton county at his home last Monday, and there before witness, he declared that he simply transferred complaints he had received from individuals to the Minister of Customs which caused my destitution without inquiry. There is the wrong! As you know, it is necessary that the member has seen personally a civil servant making politics and a declaration made to that effect, before such an employee can be dismissed without an inquiry, otherwise it is necessary to summon witnesses and give an inquiry. The member cannot fulfil that condition as he did not know me.
I am afraid that perhaps he was in error as to tlhe procedure in such cases, but I call that to the attention of the minister again because Dumoulin is, I think, a splendid example of the young men growing up in our province. He had a splendid career overseas. I was in France behind tlhe lines, where I was in perfect safety, and, time and time again, I have heard men speak in the highest words of praise of the splendid bravery of the French-Canadian corps. I have seen them in hospitals, and my heart bled for them at times. I am proud of them, and proud to represent a constituency from Quebec that was associated with such splendid bravery and valour, and therefore I take this dismissal
very much to heart; and because I believe that this young man has been wrongly treated, because I believe that he has been wrongly condemned, I think the government and parliament of this country should make tihe Utmost restitution to him that lies within theii power.

As I said yesterday, Mr. Chairman, in connection with this matter, it had already given me very considerable concern. That concern is somewhat increased by the remarks just made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I do not know that I can add a very great deal to what I said yesterday in connection with the matter.
The dismissal took place in exactly the way I stated yesterday, in accordance with the practice which has been observed for many years, and with which I may say now, I am not in very great sympathy.
Replying at once to a statement said to have been made, that no distinct charge was made to me by the member for the constituency that 'this man had exercised political partisanship, I want to say, as emphatically as I can, that such a charge was made on the part of the member that he had personal knowledge of the activities in a political way of Mr. Dumoulin. That letter is here. It is written in French, but my hon. friend is at perfect liberty to see it. It was following that, and in accordance with the established practice, that the dismissal was made. Perhaps where I may have been at fault, and I must accept any responsibility that fairly comes to me, was in this connection: A letter, I understand, was received by myself from Mr. Dumoulin taking exception to his dismissal and denying the charge. That no reply was sent to that letter, I must say is a matter of great surprise to me, because if there is one thing which I think I always do, it is at least to acknowledge any communication that is sent to me. La'ter on, however, another letter was sent to myself by the soldiers' association. That letter I did reply to, as is Shown on the file, agreeing to an investigation if the man asked for it. That the affidavits were later on sent to myself appears to be quite true. I was not in Ottawa at the time, as is shown by the file, and I did not even know the file was here until I saw it a moment ago. The receipt of those affidavits was acknowledged by my secretary who says that he submitted them to me later, which statement I do not for one moment doubt. If I at that time took no further notice of these affidavits, and no acknowledgment was made, it must have been,, I say quite frankly, because of the pressure of work due to my absence, and possibly supposing that the man had been dismissed in
Supply-National Revenue

the usual way and that nothing probably could be done. But this does stand, that I expressed myself as quite willing to have an investigation made, but also, as I said last night, I could not see exactly what remedy could be applied, because the man was out of the civil service and could only be reappointed by the Civil Service Commission itself. This may not be satisfactory to my hon. friends opposite, but last night I said I was quite willing to have another investigation made. Now I say to the committee that this morning I directed that such an investigation be made. I further directed that an order be prepared that the sum paid into the superannuation fund by Mr. Dumoulin should be refunded to him. Of course this repayment will depend on the action of the treasury board. I do not know, Mr. Chairman, that I can say any more. It is an unfortunate affair. If the investigation discloses that this officer was entirely innocent of the charge made against him, so far as I am concerned I shall do all I can to have him restored to some place in the service, if he cares to come back.

I may say to the minister
that, as I understand it, at the time this young man was dismissed there were, as we are all aware, all sorts of rumours and suspicions, due to the hiatus in the customs examination, and various firms who could have given him employment refused to do so unless he could produce a certificate of character from the department, to which he had no access. The impression went around that in some way he had been mixed up with the customs scandals, and he had to go across the border to get employment. I am instructed that the customs department should have in its records information to the effect that during the time of that campaign he had been taken away from his own office at Notre Dame des Bois and assigned to special service on the border, and was so engaged during ithe whole time that he was alleged to have been acting as a partisan in putting out this flag across the street. I think the minister might well examine into that fact. It is so stated in the man's affidavit, and I believe it to foe true.
This man was sent on relief duty at some time near the election, but the charge does not say that he was active just at the time of the election, but during the campaign.

I can well understand how
the minister might be misled, but at the time this banner was put out that is made the basis of the local charge he certainly was not there; I am sure of that.

At the moment I have no
real knowledge of the details. If the facts are as stated, the whole matter is regrettable, and I can only take the action that I have indicated.

Mr. Chairman, we
have a statement from the minister that if an investigation is held, and this returned man is proven innocent, the minister will do what he can to get him a position. I ask the house; should not that man be returned to his job, if this investigation proves that he was unfairly dismissed? All returned men will demand an answer to that question, because any of them might be treated similarly. The minister admits that it was an unwilling act on his part, that he was taken by the throat by some person.
No.

Well, the minister must admit that he did it willingly or unwillingly. He said he did not do it willingly, so he must have been forced by some influence behind the throne to treat this man in an unfair way by dismissing him from his job. I am in sympathy with what the minister has said. I may add that I commanded a unit in the first division, and in it were at least fifty or sixty French-Canadians, who could not speak English, but I am ready to declare here or in any part of t'he Dominion that I had no more loyal and no more efficient soldiers than those men. If this investigation is held and the man is found innoceint, I am confident that the returned men from one end of the country to the other will demand that he be put back on his job.

I may say to my hon. friend that so far as I am concerned, I have absolutely no power whatever-and he knows it- to restore the man to the position he held; the Civil Service Commission has that power, fortunately or unfortunately as it may be in this case. I also want to assure him in absolute sincerity that neither he nor anybody else can take me by the throat and force me to do anything that I do not desire to do.

We have nominally something over seven hundred ports, that is including outports and preventive stations. The word "port" is a misnomer in connection with some of these offices. In seventy-three of them no revenue whatever is collected, absolutely none, and in something like two hundred and sixty of them less than S500 is collected. Some capital was made out of the fact that in comparison with the United States we were away out of proportion in the number of ports throughout the country. We are; that is perfectly true, but the conditions are not exactly parallel. In the United States they have a number of stations, as they call them, in which they do make collection of revenue, but which are not classified as ports at all.
The reasons given for closing the ports are two: One is in order to save expense; the other is in order to obtain proper appraisals. It is represented, and quite rightly so, I think, that in the smaller ports it is quite impossible to have appraisers who are sufficiently skilled to make proper appraisals. The answer to that is that the frauds that were exposed during the various investigations invariably occurred in the larger ports, ports which we would not close in any case, and the remedy there is that we should have a better system of appraisals and a better staff of appraisers in these large ports. That is one of the difficulties with which we have to contend now, and that was one of the reasons why the bill was passed in the House of Commons this session, which I think will enable the department to get a better appraisal system and a better appraisal service. As a matter of fact, in about one hundred ports in this country about 96 per cent of the total customs revenue is collected. In the other six hundred ports appraisals are not much of a factor because the importations are very small. It seems to me, then, that it becomes a matter for consideration whether these small ports should be closed in order to save a very moderate expenditure, oir whether they should be maintained for the convenience of the public. It seems to me that it comes down to a decision on that point. I also think, Mr. Chairman, that the convenience of the public is a factor that should be considered.
Hear, hear.

Now, various suggestions
have been made. One, made I think by

Supply-National Revenue
Messrs. Clarkson, Gordon and Dilworth, was that the amount of revenue should be taken into consideration, and ports with a revenue of less than fifty thousand dollars a year should be closed. If that were done it would create a somewhat serious situation. I have here a list of ports with the revenues attaching to them. If we closed all ports with a revenue of less than fifty thousand dollars, we would have to close such places as Amherst, Glace Bay, Sorel, St. Mary's, Georgetown, Hanover, Kincardine, Perth, Listowel, Barrie-my hon. friend from Barrie is not in his seat-Newmarket, Swift Current, York-town, Carleton Place, Renfrew, Bracebridge, Grimsby, Orangeville, Banff,-to which my hon. friend the leader of the oposition (Mr. Bennett) objected the other day-Sydney Mines, Clinton, Wingham, Kamloops, Amprior, and a host of others which I need not mention here. It might be advisable to close some of these ports. It might also be thought advisable to close for importation purposes some of the smaller ports, leaving them open for such services as might be rendered in the clearing of vessels or for preventive purposes. As a matter of fact, many of the ports, especially in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, are really preventive stations rather than ports for the receipt of customs duties. Most of these ports are on the border. Now I think it is the desire of parliament that we keep the most careful supervision of importations from the United States. Then we have a great many ports, as I have stated, in the maritime provinces-a tremendously long coast line, a good deal more extensive than that of the United States itself. In fact, in the maritime provinces we have one hundred ports or more with revenues less than the expenditures involved in their maintenance. That would seem to be, as the lawyers say, a prima facie case for their closing; but it does not necessarily follow, because for the convenience of the public vessels have to be entered and cleared, and, as I have said, these ports do a great deal of preventive work, and they are also necessary for the promotion of the fishing industry. In western Canada we have great distances in sparsely settled country. In some instances our people are living very close to the international line but far from a customs port. On the American side there may be a town just across the border, and quite naturally and legitimately our people go over there, and it is hardly reasonable to expect them to go forty or fifty miles to reach a port of entry.
It is not easy to decide which ports should remain open and which should be closed. We did gather our inspectors together some
months ago in order to canvas the whole situation and try to arrive at some tentative decision as to what ports might be closed. The tentative list comprises some two hundred or more ports that we think might be closed, but we have not made a final decision. As a matter of fact, while the house is in session it has been very difficult to deal with matters of this kind, but this question will ibe taken up again as soon as parliament prorogues. Hon. members are familiar with the situation in their own constituencies, and I credit them with a desire to help put the Department of National Revenue on a proper basis. I invite them-not only those on this side, but on the other side as well-to suggest to me right now if they like, or by letter or otherwise, the ports in their own ridings-not in the other fellow's-which they would like to see closed.
Will you take our advice?

In conclusion I may say
that when the matter is receiving consideration all these factors will have to be very carefully gone into before a definite decision is made.

Perhaps the minister
can now give us some particulars of the regulation put into effect last fall under which magazines then on the free list became dutiable.

The ruling was made by the customs board-over which, by the way, the minister has no control whatever-on *n appeal by certain parties whose names I do not recall. The board ruled that certain publications, which the ordinary layman would call magazines, were really only works of fiction. I think that ruling was quite correct. They were of the opinion that a magazine to come strictly within that designation should have a series of articles, varied in their nature, comprising current literature, reviews, essays, perhaps some poetry and illustrations, and usually a certain amount of advertising. The board of customs therefore ruled that those so-called magazines which contained absolutely nothing but fiction, and much of it not very valuable as literature, were not strictly within the technical meaning of the word, "magazines" and were rather novels. An appeal was taken to the governor in council, and the ruling was sustained.
I am glad to have the minister s explanation, because my information is that many magazines which would not come under the class stated by him are being subjected to duty.

Then I am sure the minister would like to know that towards the end of the last navigation season there was a good deal of dissatisfaction over the lack of facilities for life saving on the upper lakes. There was a bad storm; the ice came on, and as the minister probably saw in the press there was some loss of life and a large destruction of shipping property. Would it not be advisable to consider the situation along the north shores of Georgian bay, lake Huron and lake Superior? One would think there would be need for these stations.

I shall be glad to look into the situation, but representations have been made to us that we should dispense with most of these stations. However, I am quite prepared to look into the particular case mentioned by my hon. friend.

It does look in
some cases as though this money has not been expended where it is most necessary. Cobourg is on a coal route, but at the end of the lake we have had wrecks of these coal boats running from Oswego every year, and it looks as though something further might be done. If a station were put on the islands or somewhere towards the head of the lakes

it would be more in proximity to a greajt many wrecks. I think that should be kept in mind, as at certain points there are always wrecks. Most of the wrecks at the head of the lake occur during the fall, and I think one is more necessary there than even at Cobourg. Around the Thousand Islands a number of wrecks are always occurring among the coal running boats.

What expenditures have been made during the last two or three years at the Point Pelee life saving station? I was down there two or three years ago and I understand that recommendations had been made that the track should1 be extended to the inside of the bay so that the lifeboats could be launched on the calmer side of the point in case of storm. There have been times when it has been very difficult to launch the boats during a storm.

I should like to add just a word here. There are very poor facilities for getting to the shore and back to the light house station. I think application was made to the department for better equipment, and I should like to ask the minister if he would not give serious consideration to providing better equipment for that crew. There should be some kind of launch provided rather than a rowboat. They have some distance to go, and sometimes the storms are very severe.
These representations have been considered, and I will be prepared to look into the situation in that particular place.
Is it the intention of the government to place anything in the estimates this session for the life saving station at Scatarie island?

According to the information which I can obtain, this station is adequately equipped. We have provided practically everything we can provide, but in view of the interest my hon. friend, is taking in this matter I shall be pleased to consider the suggestion that he has made.

I am pleased to note that the minister is interesting himself in the condition of the life saving station at Scatarie island. I visited Scatarie island in 1926, a short time after the ship Ringhorn grounded off that coast and five lives were lost. I had a conversation with the captain and he told me that he remained on the ship all night. He could see the people on the shore as they built fires, and he waited all night for some method of bringing his people ashore. I claim that we should at least

Private Bills
have a gun on this island in order that a line might be fired on board ship. Had such provision been provided for the island at that time, these five lives would have been saved.
I also visited the life saving station at that time. I understand that the members of this station are volunteers, only receiving pay when they go out on a life saving trip. I looked over the boat, and it was not seaworthy. It had been in the quarters for years, and I know that no man would risk his life in ordinary weather in the lifeboat that was provided for Scatarie island, let alone go out in a storm to take a crew off a ship. I am bringing this matter to the attention of the department because more lives have been lost on Scatarie island during the last ten years than on any other part of the Atlantic coast. It is known to-day, like Sable island, as one of the graveyards of the Atlantic. I bring this matter forcibly to the attention of the government, that human lives could have been saved if the proper equipment had been installed at that point.
I also wish to bring to the attention of the government the question, and inquire whether they have any additional information regarding it, as to the fog whistle or signal on the western coast of Scatarie island. I brought this question up some time ago.

I am informed that inquiries were made regarding this matter, and our information is that everything is in good order, and that the fog alarm is functioning regularly. That is the information we have in the department, having made inquiries.

We know that the fog alarm is functioning regularly, but the point is that ships sailing in a westerly direction cannot hear that fog horn two miles from the light. The fog whistle is at the lighthouse at Scatarie island. I have an article here from the Halifax Chronicle, the Liberal organ of my friends from the province of Nova Scotia I will read a paragraph:
Scatarie has been the graveyard of many a staunch ship, and according to seamen of Main-a-Dieu, this barren coast will claim many another victim, unless a new system of signals is inaugurated.
The fishermen claim that when approaching that island in a westerly direction, sailing from Louisburg to Scatarie island, they cannot hear that fog whistle two miles from the station. On the eastern side they can hear it for ten or twelve miles, but every wreck that has occurred on that coast during the last tea years has occurred on the western side of the island, as a result of thick fog, and not being
able to hear the fog whistle. In view of what has happened during the last few years I think the minister should make a very thorough investigation, and should at least inquire of the fishermen on that coast, who are the people concerned.

I will do so.
